History:
• Chief complaint: Progressive, intermittent decreased hearing in the left ear for ~6 weeks.  
• Course: Begins and resolves intermittently; similar brief episode ~1 year ago (2 days only).  
• Laterality: Unilateral ‒ left ear only; right ear normal.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in left ear, less noticeable when background TV/music is on.  
  – Occasional mild disequilibrium/“off-balance” sensation; no true vertigo or spinning; brief nausea reported.  
• Negatives: No ear pain, discharge, itching, fever, chest pain, palpitations.  
• Triggers/relievers: Tinnitus masked by ambient sound; no cotton-bud use; no known trauma or infection reported.

Past Medical History:
• Prior brief (2-day) episode of left-sided hearing difficulty ~1 year ago.  
• Chronic illnesses: Not recorded.  
• Allergies: Not recorded.  
• Medications: None reported (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Surgical/hospital history, family/social history: Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
• Visual inspection/otoscopy: Not performed during video visit.  
• General appearance: Appears well; conversant via video.  
• Vital signs, neurologic, head & neck exam: Not recorded.

Impression:
Unilateral left-sided hearing loss with tinnitus and mild disequilibrium. Most likely conductive etiology pending otoscopic exam.  
Top differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript):  
1. Cerumen impaction – common, reversible cause; clinician plans to rule out first.  
2. Serous otitis media / Eustachian-tube dysfunction – could explain fluctuating conductive loss and tinnitus without pain.  
3. Ménière’s disease – less likely but considered given hearing loss + tinnitus + imbalance.

Management Plan:
• Arrange face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic evaluation of the left ear to check for wax or other obstruction.  
• Provide patient with tinnitus education leaflet (link placed in visit notes).  
• Administrative: Clinician to message support team to schedule appointment; patient to call support number to confirm slot.  
• Safety-netting: If symptoms worsen or new issues arise before in-person review, patient advised to book another video consult.  

Patient Summary:
32-year-old man with 6-week history of intermittent left-ear hearing loss, tinnitus, and mild disequilibrium. No pain or discharge. Plan is in-person otoscopy to exclude cerumen impaction or other conductive cause; patient given tinnitus information and scheduling instructions.

Key Takeaways:
• Attend in-person appointment this week for ear examination.  
• Read supplied tinnitus leaflet to understand condition and coping strategies.  
• Re-contact service promptly if hearing suddenly worsens, vertigo develops, or other concerns arise.

Next Steps:
• Otoscopic exam; treat cerumen impaction if present (e.g., removal, cerumenolytics).  
• If ear canal clear, consider audiometry and ENT referral for further assessment (e.g., Ménière’s, ET dysfunction).  
• Document allergies and medication list at next visit.
